The algorithm a code model writes behaves like an almost discrete decision taken at one or two tokens early in the program, and temperature acts on that decision only through the next-token distribution there; a push of the task specification states acts upstream, on the states that set that distribution (Section~\\ref{sec:res-sets}). This single account explains the three regimes we observed. Where post-training has widened the fork margin to 4.85 to 17.04 nats, a temperature of 1.3 cannot reach the alternative, so the algorithm is fixed while every other position, where the next token is less certain, varies more. That is the phrasing growth of Figure~\\ref{fig:phrasings}. Where the forking token is contested, temperature sharpens or flattens the same two or three known algorithms at the rate the forking-token logits predict. And where the model reaches the decision through many openings, as Llama does on the grid task, the choice is spread over the opening and no law at a single token captures it. In the terms of the question that motivates this work, a tight temperature with top-$k$ 10 gives one idea in a few phrasings, and a loose one gives the same idea, or the same few ideas, in more phrasings.\n\nThis account reconciles two findings that look contradictory. \\citet{Lee2025} report that temperature above 1 raises algorithmic diversity among correct programs, and we find that temperature never changes the algorithm on default tasks. Both hold. On tasks whose fork is contested, temperature moves mass between known algorithms at the predicted rate; Prim on minimum spanning tree weight rises from 0.07 at $T = 0.3$ to 0.31 at $T = 1.3$. On tasks whose fork is decided by several nats, it does not. A diversity evaluation that pools tasks will see an average of the two. Our results also bear on the claim that a model returns the average answer and that only context moves it elsewhere. The instruct default is not the base model's average: post-training moved and sharpened one token, often promoting the base model's second or third choice, and left the repertoire unchanged.\n\nFor practice, the account says where to spend randomness. Temperature is a poor exploration control for algorithm choice, and on contested units its effect can be predicted before sampling from the forking-token logits. Controls that act upstream of the fork, such as context that implies an algorithm, a prompt that lists approaches and then picks one, or perturbations of the task specification states, do change the algorithm, but they move it to the second choice the model already knows, and at a cost in correctness. The audits found no route from any control applied to single samples to a correct novel algorithm. An evaluator that keeps improvements across generations made the same 8B model better than the textbook rule on bin packing, which is where the field's discovery systems operate~\\citep{RomeraParedes2023,Novikov2025}. Whether it made the model new remains open after the replication found none.\n\nFor interpretability, the results suggest that readouts of a plan taken before the code starts should be validated against the forking token. Natural language and sparse-feature readouts found no verbalised plan before the code, and fitted subspace edits at the fork moved the algorithm without passing the controls that would make them a variable of the model, consistent with the interpretability illusions that subspace patching can produce~\\citep{Makelov2023}. The forking token is where intervention is cheap and measurable, but a certified mechanism for the choice is still missing.\n\n\\section{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\nThe headline contrast between the push and temperature ran only in an 8-bit (W8A8) engine and was not rerun in bfloat16; the push alone changes the algorithm in bfloat16 at the same absolute push norm, but the paired contrast was not repeated, and it pools two tasks, with the grid task moving only 2.50 of 20 seeds. Most results come from one model, Qwen3-8B, in non-thinking mode. The composed law was tested on three held-out units in two other families; two passed and Llama's grid task failed, below the four held-out units the preregistered claim required, so the law's generality is an open question. The law was also not clearly better than the flat law, a baseline that predicts no change (four of six units, sign test $p = 0.34$), which means that much of its accuracy reflects how little temperature moves these units. The temperature null on shared seeds rests on 20 seeds per task, which bounds the change rate per seed below 0.17 per task, not at zero, and it ran with 8-bit linear layers; the bfloat16 fork margins and the grid sweep with independent samples agree with it, but the thinking-mode evidence is limited to shortest path and a 10-seed grid arm.\n\nThe tasks are short, well-known programming problems whose solutions are likely memorised, with catalogues of three to ten known algorithms; the conclusions may not hold for open-ended programs or for problems without a textbook solution. Experiments ran on different engines (bfloat16 and 8-bit linear layers, vLLM and Hugging Face); push escapes reproduced in bfloat16, but pushed cells showed precision sensitivity at the level of single streams. Phrasing clusters depend on a Jaccard threshold over AST shingles with normalised identifiers, and the growth was driven mostly by the grid task.\n\nLabels and the novelty audit carry their own uncertainty. Labellers were gated per task, but the gate failed by its strict criteria for the decoding experiment with independent samples and for the agreement between runtime and AST labels on the path tasks ($\\kappa = 0.753$), and the expansion-order tracer used for the ban of five names failed its gold gate, so those numbers are descriptive. In the program search no LLM judge passed its control gate, so novelty there rests on manual reads, and one reader's eight candidates were not reproduced by the replication. The geometry in activation space is correlational, and the map built from names is confounded by lexical overlap between algorithm names.\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\\label{sec:conclusion}\n\nOn the same random streams, a random push of Qwen3-8B's task specification states changed the algorithm in more seeds than temperature did, by 0.545 per seed (95\\% CI 0.41 to 0.67) over shortest path and $k$-th smallest, a preregistered contrast that held in an 8-bit engine and is untested in bfloat16. Temperature from 0.3 to 1.3 left the default algorithm unchanged in all 60 seeds (20 per task) while phrasings multiplied, because a forking token, not temperature, chooses the algorithm. Fork margins of 4.85 to 17.04 nats on the default tasks, widened by post-training, account for the null, and on contested forks the forking-token logits committed before sampling predicted the temperature response within 0.014 to 0.054 total variation on five of six units. No control we tested produced a correct algorithm outside the known repertoire.\n\nFuture work follows directly:\n\\begin{itemize}\n  \\item testing the composed law on more held-out units and families, including models that reach the fork through many openings;\n  \\item extending the forking-token analysis to thinking traces, where the first approach named was fixed in every trace we read;\n  \\item spending sampling randomness at forking tokens inside program search, and measuring whether it buys ideas rather than phrasings;\n  \\item searching for a variable of the algorithm choice that passes controls with permuted labels and with randomly initialised networks.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\section*{Code and Data Availability}\n\nCode, prompts, raw generations, algorithm labels and the preregistration hash chains of every experiment are public at \\url{https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-295f8e-prompt-bans-substitute-not-just-subtract}; the footnotes in Sections~\\ref{sec:intro} to~\\ref{sec:results} link each result to the code that produced it.\n\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\end{document}\n", "numLines": 100, "startLine": 259, "totalLines": 358}}

```
{"stdout": "\\section{What the run learned overall, and what is still open}\n\\label{sec:closing}\nThis closing section is the draft's own synthesis, written after iteration 10; the open questions it lists are collected again, with the bookkeeping, in Section~\\ref{sec:open}.\n\nAfter ten iterations the run has a firm picture of the collapse, a measured place where the algorithm is decided in generation, a law that predicts what temperature does there, and a weight-level account of how post-training wrote the default at that place. It has internal handles in two families that move the algorithm without being the model's own variable, a measured and model-dependent gap between obeying a ban by name and obeying it by mechanism, and an answer to the request's question about truly novel solutions: an executable evaluator makes the model write heuristics better than the textbook rule, but no route in the run produced a confirmed new algorithm or heuristic. One reader classed eight bin-packing programs from one search as a new idea, and the independent replication found none.\n\nQwen3-8B [5] writes BFS and Dijkstra almost without exception on the two path search tasks and one algorithm on each of 13 further coding tasks (modal share 1.00 on 12, 0.98 on one). The collapse is not universal. Three of 15 new tasks are already mixed in the instruct twin (trapped rain water, minimum spanning tree weight and valid anagram, with minority shares of 0.13 to 0.36), and on two of them the instruct model is more diverse than its base model. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [22] attempts more algorithms, but its correct grid programs are BFS 20 of 20; gemma-3-4b-it [76] writes DFS in about 70\\% and BFS in about 30\\% of programs for one grid prompt; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [124] shares most of Qwen3-8B's defaults. On the grid task eight more open configurations (Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with thinking on and off, Qwen3-8B with thinking on, gemma-3-27b-it, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in bfloat16) write BFS or DFS at baseline apart from a few programs labelled other or invalid, and so does gpt-oss-120b [152] (BFS 45, DFS 5 of 50). The collapse extends to online bin packing for the reasoning models: asked once for a priority function, Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with thinking write best fit in 50 of 50 and 48 of 49 valid programs, while Qwen3-8B without thinking spreads (25 of its 36 valid programs are outside the six-rule catalogue and 9 are best fit). So the answer to the request's question whether the model always designs BFS is: on the grid, BFS or DFS nearly always, with the split fixed by the model; on weighted shortest path, Dijkstra; on bin packing, best fit for the thinking models.\n\nThe algorithm is decided at one or two generated tokens after a shared opening, the fork, where one can be found. On the mixed units programs share an opening of 18 to 61 tokens and the next token settles the algorithm: ' Kr' or ' Prim' on minimum spanning tree weight, ' n' or ' left' on trapped rain water, ' visited' against a blank line or ' queue' in Gemma. The entropy of the algorithm given the fork token's class is at most 0.19 bits as iteration 7 measured it, at most 0.004 bits on the five Qwen3-8B and Gemma units of iteration 8's blind locator, and 0.63 bits on Llama's grid task, where the fork is reached through many openings. Prefix resampling finds these forks blind on mixed units in Qwen3-8B and Gemma, but not on a collapsed task, where resampling at T 1 never leaves the default. The fork's entropy lies above the 90th percentile of the twin's per-token entropy in all 209 twin samples that reach it, though it can be small in absolute terms (median 0.13 nats on connected components), and it is the single highest-entropy position among the first 64 tokens on most slots of three units but on 2 of 50 and 0 of 37 slots of the other two. On kth smallest a ban decides before the first generated token, and on shortest path no single token decides within 60 tokens. Thought anchors and forks, the logit and tuned lenses and a Jacobian lens were all run on this question; the lenses found no veto layer at the commitment token, because the fork has already happened at the first token. Inside an evaluator search, whether new heuristics are born at single decision tokens is not settled: forcing the argmax back at an offspring's birth token reverted it to a parent's behaviour at 0.50 against 0.26 at random positions in one search and 0.40 against 0.36 in the other.\n\nTemperature acts on the algorithm through those one or two tokens and reweights ideas the fork already weighs. A law composed over the forks, committed before sampling from teacher-forced logits, predicted the minority share across T 0.3 to 1.3 within a mean total variation distance of 0.029 to 0.054 on three Qwen3-8B units and of 0.033 and 0.014 on two held-out Gemma units; it beats the flat law on 4 of 6 units only (sign test p 0.34), and on Llama's grid task every predictor fails (0.142). Applying temperature only at the fork moves the mix as predicted and raises correct-only Hill-1 on valid anagram from 1.78 to 2.78 at a 2-point pass cost, but on collapsed connected components it reaches DFS in at most 18\\% of programs. Forcing each of the fork's top 64 tokens reaches one more known idea on three units, each about once in 2 million to 50 million samples at T 1. Lowering T from 1.0 to 0.3 moves the output toward the default, and top-k 10 gives the same programs as top-p 1 because every fork token lies in the top 10. On the collapsed tasks fork margins of 4.85 to 17.04 nats put the alternative out of reach, which is why iterations 1 to 4 changed the algorithm in 0 of 20 seeds under a shared seed while phrasings multiplied. The answer to question 1a to 1c of the request is that a model has few ideas at tight temperature and the same few at loose temperature, in proportions its fork logits fix, with more phrasings of each as T rises; it is case (a), not case (b), and loosening temperature does not turn one idea into several on a collapsed task. Inside a search temperature is not a reliable exploration knob either. Under one prompt, temperature 1.6 with top-p 0.95 found 373 behaviours in 4,000 calls; under a prompt that invites copying the parent, it became greedy and found one; on TSP it halved validity. Temperature is not the creativity knob the request asks about.\n\nContext seeding does not change the algorithm. Under a random entropy seed prepended to the prompt the grid task stays BFS 100 and shortest path Dijkstra 100, and in a later cell both random seeds give Dijkstra in 30 of 30 programs; the word seed moves the read-position state 1.555 times the paraphrase noise without changing the program. Prompt instructions change claims more than algorithms. Of 574 outputs with a claim record under the long novelty instructions, 484 claimed a new algorithm and 220 of the 295 with code were catalogue algorithms. On bin packing the short novelty instruction (a one-line request to make a new algorithm) returns best fit in 28 of 29 and 28 of 28 programs from the two thinking models, and every program that claims novelty there is a known rule or a corpus heuristic. Inside an evaluator search the picture changes: an instruction to use an idea different from both parents is obeyed in behaviour, lowers the share of offspring that rename a parent (0.44 against 0.86, 0.67 against 0.96, 0.06 against 0.18 to 0.22) and found the most behaviours in two of three searches. An instruction to differ works when there is something to differ from.\n\nPost-training made the fork margins, and the instruct default is a sharpened choice of the base model, not its mean answer. On the three collapsed Qwen3-8B tasks the instruct fork margin exceeds the base model's by 2.1 to 13.4 nats while phrasing entropy moves by under 0.5 nats, and the default is the base model's second or third choice at the fork. In Gemma the grid fork gains 1.78 nats and post-training reversed and concentrated the base model's preference (base P(BFS) 0.25, 0.663 of base mass unmapped), while the first-and-last-position forks sharpen the base model's own first choice. That post-training shifts concentrate at forks of high base entropy is shown by Cantarero et al. [142] and Sparse but Critical [143], and the run confirms the confound they control: at Gemma's forks the base-instruct divergence is only 0.75 to 1.18 times that of positions matched for base entropy. What the run adds is the algorithm-level outcome on code at counterfactually located forks, and where the sharpening is written in Qwen3-8B. It is not written upstream at the task-specification nodes. In activations it sits at the fork, in late MLPs and in the unembedding, which alone carries 0.43 of the minimum spanning tree gap and 0.85 of the connected components gap. In weights, restoring the base rows of the three fork-class tokens of connected components closes 0.548 of the gap, almost all through the alternatives' rows (0.489 against 0.060): post-training suppressed the readout of ' dfs' and ' bfs' more than it boosted ' find'. The effect is readout-level but not token-specific, because random edits of the same size confined to the residual's top 64 directions do as much (p 0.37). Swapping the late MLPs (layers 26 to 35) back to base does not close the gap, while matched early swaps close 0.461, so no specific late-MLP store of the default was found. At the same three rows, the edit is also a cheap lever over which known algorithm gets written: at dose 1 it gives correct DFS in 21 of 90 slots against 4 of 90, and at two and three times the delta in 21 and 30 of 30, with every program passing; on minimum spanning tree 24 to 27 of 30 programs become correct Prim. Splicing the base model's fork logits (Fork-Patched Decoding [142]) gives 15 of 30. No edit produced a correct program outside the known classes. To the request's hypothesis that the model gives the mean answer and only context pushes it into another subspace, the run's answer is that the default is a sharpened, not\n\nA random displacement of the task specification states at early to middle blocks changes the algorithm in Qwen3-8B, and its size has to be counted in the right unit. At the absolute unit of iteration 4, bfloat16 escapes on 26 of 40 directions on connected components and 6 of 40 on shortest path, close to the 8-bit engine's 29 and 8. These pushes do not act through any fitted subspace: their projection on the task band's DAS subspace associates with their escapes at Spearman 0.09, and clamping the subspace back to the twin removes none of 218 escapes. Internal handles exist in both families, and under one protocol none is a certified variable. A rank-4 DAS edit at the fork is a sufficient handle in Gemma (22 of 30 correct BFS against 6 unedited) and no handle at Qwen3-8B's fork, where the edit toward BFS writes BFS in 29 of 30 programs and 24 fail; neither passes the specificity controls, and both show the off-manifold overshoot Makelov et al. warn of [122]. Path-patching circuits for the fork margin show a late stack of fork-position MLPs and heads carrying the fork logit in both families, with different motifs; steering the top five Qwen3-8B nodes rewrites the algorithm with every program passing, but matched random components do nearly as much at the committed dose, and most matched random patching sets repeat a component. The layer-0 condition-span MLP gives about 7.9 nats on the five forced held-out prompts and about 0 on the five padded twins. Specificity fails at the same late fork-position sites under steering, DAS, cross-model patching and, at the readout, row edits. Sparse autoencoder features read Gemma's fork (R-squared 0.66 against 0.18 for text) but steer it less than a difference-in-means direction, and a natural language autoencoder on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct names the algorithm only where the prompt names it. Natural BFS against DFS internals were read within a ban in Qwen3-8B and within one prompt in Gemma, with circuits for the fork in both.\n\nA single prompt ban, where the model obeys it, removes the default and the output collapses on one replacement: Bellman-Ford\\slash{}SPFA on shortest path, DFS on the grid, and quickselect, a size-k heap, brute force, index marking and BFS on the bench tasks where Qwen3-8B obeys; on bin packing, banning best fit sent Qwen3-32B to first fit in 14 of 30 programs and outside the catalogue in 16. Shown a correct program of another algorithm and told not to use it, the model goes home to its default. How often a ban is obeyed depends on its wording more than on anything else measured. A ban of the whole repertoire is answered in two ways, depending on the model and the task. On the grid, read by the runtime label (heap priorities, frontier evidence, restarts) and by the expansion-order tracer over 546 programs in ten configurations, lexical compliance exceeds mechanistic compliance by 0.70 or 0.61 (0.66 if unit-weight Dijkstra, IDA* and jump point search count as compliant), in every configuration; the tracer failed its gold gate on iterative deepening, so these numbers are descriptive. Under cumulative bans of one to five names, Qwen3-14B with thinking renames under every reading except the fine tracer on held-out templates, while Qwen3-32B with thinking moves mostly to other known disciplines (by hand reads 0.59 mechanistically compliant at five names, against 0.22 by the runtime label). On bin packing, read by exact behaviour, Qwen3-8B without thinking renames (lexical 0.91 against mechanistic 0.51 at five names; about half its lexically clean programs are still a banned rule, mostly best fit under invented names such as \\emph{tightest fit}), while Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with thinking obey and leave the catalogue (gaps +0.04 and -0.13). Thinking traces name the banned rule in every cell. Renaming is therefore not a fixed property of a model: the same reasoning model renames the banned algorithm on the grid and obeys on bin packing. A ban described without names moved grid compliance by an instrument-dependent amount (+0.58 by the runtime label, -0.07 by the tracer, about +0.21 under the per-cell reading), and on bin packing the test could not be built, because the models named only one description correctly.\n\nThe answer to the request's top-five question, edge or opposite, depends on the map and on the survivor. By hand reads of 76 survivors of the grid ban, 0.30 are unit-weight Dijkstra, which is BFS order on a unit grid, and the rest are known algorithms with other disciplines (grid Bellman-Ford rounds, heaps keyed by goal-independent coordinates, random frontiers). On every manifold built from language (named prompts, name-only sentences and name-free descriptions the model names correctly) unit-weight Dijkstra lies opposite the banned five (g 1.63, 1.20 and 1.08 times the median of the non-banned algorithms); the language manifolds track lexical distance between the names and textbook data-structure attributes, not measured expansion order. On the manifold built from name-scrubbed programs it lies at the edge (0.67), its iteration-8 survivors place at the edge, and the Bellman-Ford\\slash{}SPFA survivors place opposite on both gate-passing Qwen3-32B frames. The factorial program set of iteration 10 shows what that program map encodes: container more than expansion discipline (partial correlations 0.300 and 0.414 against 0.226 and 0.285) and token surface more than both. # Paper assembly and final review
```

````
This folder holds the run's publishable outputs (the paper, its web page and interactive
companion, the internal research report and its executive summary) and the independent final
review that checked every output against the run's artifact files before publication.

## What the final review did

- Traced the paper's numbers to the artifacts' result files (same-seed contrast, temperature
  null, phrasing counts, temperature-law errors, base-versus-instruct margins, task-state
  exchange, ban screens, bin-packing and TSP searches, program-map factorial).
- Narrowed claims that the artifacts contradicted: the novelty statement (one bin-packing search's
  manual read classed eight programs as a new idea, not reproduced by its replication), the
  practical reading of decision-token branching in program search (it did not reliably beat
  forcing at a random position, and failed on TSP), the composition of the five-name-ban
  survivors (6 of 17 unit-weight Dijkstra, 7 Bellman-Ford/SPFA), the alias test wording, the
  judge-gate wording, and added the program-map factorial result.
- Fixed a bibliography entry printed in capitals, credited the inspiration repository, rounded two
  raw floats in the executive summary, and brought the web page and interactive page into line.
- Rebuilt the paper and the executive summary and re-rendered every changed page.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `paper/` | The paper as published (`paper.tex`, `paper.pdf`, `references.bib`, `references.json`), its web page `index.html`, the interactive page `interactive.html` and the figures. |
| `paper/workspace/` | Build folder of the paper; `build.sh` rebuilds `paper.pdf`. |
| `report.pdf`, `exec_summary.pdf` | The internal research report and its executive summary. |
| `report_workspace/` | Build folder of the report and the executive summary. |
| `report_latex/` | LaTeX source of the report as published. |
| `final_review/` | The review: `checks_before.md`, `readme_preview.md`, and `scratch/` with page renders, screenshots, the bibliography check and the edit scripts. |
| `run_record/` | The run record the paper and report were written from. |
| `.aii/manifest.yaml` | Storage decisions: no entries, because no file here is a large binary or cache. |

## Rebuilding

```bash
# Paper (pdflatex, bibtex, pdflatex, pdflatex)
bash paper/workspace/build.sh

# Executive summary
cd report_workspace && pdflatex exec_summary.tex && pdflatex exec_summary.tex
```

Open `paper/index.html` or `paper/interactive.html` in a browser to view the pages; they load
nothing from the network.

## Restoring removed files

No files were marked for deletion, so nothing needs to be restored.
EOF
ls -la README.md .aii/
````
